Direct-Current Circuits

Kirchhoff's rules, networks & RC transients

← PSE II Course

27.0 — Reading the Circuit

In Chapter 26, we learned the language of circuits — current, resistance, and power. We analyzed a single resistor connected to a battery and found that Ohm’s Law governs the relationship. But a single resistor and a single battery is the simplest possible circuit. Real devices — your phone, your car’s electrical system, the power grid itself — involve networks of elements that cannot be reduced by inspection alone.

The answers come from Gustav Robert Kirchhoff (1824–1887), who in 1845 — as a 21-year-old student at the University of Königsberg — published two deceptively simple rules that formalize what we already know about charge and energy conservation. His junction rule says charge cannot pile up at a node; his loop rule says potential is single-valued. Together, they reduce any circuit, no matter how complex, to a system of linear equations.

“The algebraic sum of the currents at any junction point is zero; the algebraic sum of the potential differences around any closed loop is zero.” — Gustav Kirchhoff, 1845

Series and parallel combinations, batteries with internal resistance, multi-battery networks, and RC circuits all yield to the same two rules. This chapter develops those tools and applies them to increasingly realistic circuits.

*Personal note: Kirchhoff was 21 when he published these rules. They remain, nearly two centuries later, the foundation of every circuit analysis course in the world. Simplicity, when it captures the right physics, is timeless.

27.1 — EMF and Internal Resistance

The Electromotive Force

In Chapter 26, we treated batteries as ideal sources of constant potential difference. The electromotive force (EMF), denoted \(\mathcal{E}\), is the maximum potential difference a battery can maintain when no current flows. Despite its name, EMF is not a force — it is a voltage. The term is historical, inherited from a time before the distinction between force and energy was precise.

Real Batteries and Terminal Voltage

A real battery has internal resistance \(r\) — the resistance of the chemicals and electrodes through which the current must pass. We model a real battery as an ideal EMF source \(\mathcal{E}\) in series with \(r\):

When current \(I\) flows, some EMF is “used up” driving current through the internal resistance. The terminal voltage is:

\[\boxed{\Delta V = \mathcal{E} - Ir}\]

Applying the loop rule to the full circuit gives the current:

\[\boxed{I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R + r}}\]

The Compressed Air Analogy

A compressed air canister provides a useful physical picture. The canister’s internal pressure is the EMF (\(\mathcal{E}\)) — the maximum driving force available. The nozzle restricts the flow: a narrow nozzle (high \(R\)) lets little air escape and maintains nearly full pressure at the outlet. Opening the nozzle wider (decreasing \(R\)) allows more flow but drops the outlet pressure because more of the canister’s pressure is “used up” pushing air through the canister’s own internal passages (the internal resistance \(r\)). At maximum nozzle opening (\(R \to 0\)), the flow rate is as high as the canister can sustain (\(I = \mathcal{E}/r\)), but the outlet pressure drops to zero — all the pressure is lost internally. This is exactly the short-circuit condition: \(\Delta V = \mathcal{E} - Ir \to 0\).

Ideal vs. Real Batteries

Property Ideal Battery Real Battery
Internal resistance \(r = 0\) \(r > 0\)
Terminal voltage \(\Delta V = \mathcal{E}\) \(\Delta V = \mathcal{E} - Ir\)
Power to load \(P = \mathcal{E}I\) \(P = \mathcal{E}I - I^2r\)
Short-circuit current (\(R = 0\)) \(\infty\) \(\mathcal{E}/r\) (finite)

The short-circuit result is physically important: a real battery cannot deliver infinite current. If you connect a wire directly across its terminals, the maximum current is \(I_\text{max} = \mathcal{E}/r\), and all the battery’s power is dissipated internally as heat. This is why short circuits are dangerous.

Example: Terminal Voltage Under Load and Aging

A battery has \(\mathcal{E} = 12.0\ \text{V}\) and internal resistance \(r = 0.050\ \Omega\). It is connected to a load \(R = 3.00\ \Omega\).

Current: \(I = 12.0/(3.00 + 0.050) = 3.93\ \text{A}\)

Terminal voltage: \(\Delta V = 12.0 - (3.93)(0.050) = \boxed{11.8\ \text{V}}\)

Power budget: \(P_R = I^2R = 46.3\ \text{W}\) (to load), \(P_r = I^2r = 0.77\ \text{W}\) (internal). The battery is 98% efficient.

But if the battery ages and \(r\) rises to \(2.00\ \Omega\): current drops to \(2.40\ \text{A}\), terminal voltage falls to \(7.2\ \text{V}\), and internal loss climbs to \(11.5\ \text{W}\) — nearly 40% of the battery’s output is now wasted as heat. This is why old batteries “die” even though their EMF hasn’t changed much.

*Personal note: This is why car batteries feel warm after cranking a starter motor. The starter draws hundreds of amps, and \(I^2r\) losses are substantial. It’s also why jump-starting works — the second battery shares the current load, reducing \(I^2r\) losses in each.

27.2 — Resistors in Series and Parallel

Series Combination

When resistors are connected end-to-end, the same current \(I\) flows through each one. The voltage drops add:

\[\boxed{R_\text{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \cdots} \qquad \text{(series)}\]

The equivalent resistance is always larger than the largest individual resistor. Adding resistors in series is like extending a pipe — more friction, less flow.

Parallel Combination

When resistors share the same two nodes, they have the same voltage. The currents split:

\[\boxed{\frac{1}{R_\text{eq}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} + \cdots} \qquad \text{(parallel)}\]

The equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor. Adding resistors in parallel is like adding lanes to a highway — more paths, less overall resistance.

Two-resistor shortcut: \(R_\text{eq} = R_1 R_2/(R_1 + R_2)\)

The Grand Comparison — Capacitors vs. Resistors

This is the single most important table in this chapter. Notice how every rule is reversed:

Property Capacitors (Ch 25) Resistors (Ch 27)
Defining equation \(C = Q/\Delta V\) \(R = \Delta V/I\)
Geometry formula \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\) \(R = \rho\ell/A\)
Material parameter \(\varepsilon\) (permittivity) \(\rho\) (resistivity)
Larger area → Larger \(C\) Smaller \(R\)
Series rule \(1/C_\text{eq} = \sum 1/C_i\) \(R_\text{eq} = \sum R_i\)
Parallel rule \(C_\text{eq} = \sum C_i\) \(1/R_\text{eq} = \sum 1/R_i\)
Same quantity in series Charge \(Q\) Current \(I\)
Same quantity in parallel Voltage \(\Delta V\) Voltage \(\Delta V\)
Series: equivalent is… Smaller than smallest Larger than largest
Parallel: equivalent is… Larger than largest Smaller than smallest

Why are the rules reversed? The defining equations are reciprocals of each other: \(C \propto Q/\Delta V\) while \(R \propto \Delta V/I\). When you connect elements in series, the conserved quantity flows through each element. For capacitors in series, the conserved quantity is charge \(Q\), leading to the reciprocal rule. For resistors in series, the conserved quantity is current \(I\), leading to direct addition.

Example: A Mixed Resistor Network

\(R_1 = 8.0\ \Omega\) and \(R_2 = 4.0\ \Omega\) are in series. \(R_3 = 6.0\ \Omega\) and \(R_4 = 3.0\ \Omega\) are in parallel. These two sub-networks are then connected in series across \(\Delta V = 42\ \text{V}\).

Series pair: \(R_{12} = 8.0 + 4.0 = 12.0\ \Omega\)

Parallel pair: \(1/R_{34} = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 3/6.0\), so \(R_{34} = 2.0\ \Omega\)

Final series: \(R_\text{eq} = 12.0 + 2.0 = \boxed{14.0\ \Omega}\)

Current: \(I = 42/14.0 = 3.0\ \text{A}\) through \(R_1\) and \(R_2\), splitting at the parallel junction: \(I_3 = \boxed{1.0\ \text{A}}\), \(I_4 = \boxed{2.0\ \text{A}}\).

Check: \(\Delta V_{12} + \Delta V_{34} = (3.0)(12.0) + (1.0)(6.0) = 36 + 6.0 = 42\ \text{V}\) ✓

27.3 — Kirchhoff’s Rules

When Series and Parallel Aren’t Enough

Many circuits cannot be decomposed into simple series and parallel combinations. A circuit with two batteries of different EMFs may drive current into one battery (charging it) while drawing current from the other. No amount of series/parallel reduction can handle this.

The Junction Rule (Kirchhoff’s Current Law — KCL)

At any junction in a circuit:

\[\boxed{\sum I_\text{in} = \sum I_\text{out}}\]

This is charge conservation. In steady state, charge does not accumulate at any point.

The Loop Rule (Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law — KVL)

Around any closed loop:

\[\boxed{\sum \Delta V = 0}\]

This is energy conservation. Electric potential is single-valued: if you walk around any closed path and return to your starting point, the net change in potential must be zero.

Sign Conventions

Element Traversed Direction \(\Delta V\)
Resistor \(R\) With assumed current \(I\) \(-IR\)
Resistor \(R\) Against assumed current \(I\) \(+IR\)
EMF source \(\mathcal{E}\) From \(-\) to \(+\) (through source) \(+\mathcal{E}\)
EMF source \(\mathcal{E}\) From \(+\) to \(-\) (through source) \(-\mathcal{E}\)

The sign convention is bookkeeping, not physics. You can assume any direction for any current. If your assumption is wrong, the algebra will return a negative value — which simply means the actual current flows opposite to your assumed direction.

Problem-Solving Strategy

  1. Label branch currents with assumed directions. If wrong, the algebra returns a negative value.
  2. Apply the junction rule at enough junctions. For \(J\) junctions, you get \(J - 1\) independent equations.
  3. Apply the loop rule around independent loops. For \(B\) branches and \(J\) junctions, you need \(B - (J - 1)\) loop equations.
  4. Solve the system of linear equations. Verify with an unused loop.

*Personal note: Kirchhoff’s rules reduce circuit analysis to linear algebra. The skill is choosing the most convenient junctions and loops, not in the physics itself. The physics is just charge conservation and energy conservation.

Example: A Two-Battery Network

\(\mathcal{E}_1 = 18.0\ \text{V}\), \(\mathcal{E}_2 = 12.0\ \text{V}\), \(R_1 = 4.0\ \Omega\), \(R_2 = 6.0\ \Omega\), \(R_3 = 8.0\ \Omega\). Find the current in each branch.

Junction rule (top): \(I_1 = I_2 + I_3\) — (Eq. 1)

Loop 1 (left, counterclockwise): \(+\mathcal{E}_1 - I_1 R_1 - I_3 R_3 = 0\)

\[18.0 - 4.0\,I_1 - 8.0\,I_3 = 0 \qquad \text{(Eq. 2)}\]

Loop 2 (right, counterclockwise): \(-\mathcal{E}_2 - I_2 R_2 + I_3 R_3 = 0\)

\[-12.0 - 6.0\,I_2 + 8.0\,I_3 = 0 \qquad \text{(Eq. 3)}\]

Solving: Substitute Eq. 1 into Eq. 2, then Eq. 3:

\[\boxed{I_3 = 1.50\ \text{A}}, \quad \boxed{I_2 = 0.00\ \text{A}}, \quad \boxed{I_1 = 1.50\ \text{A}}\]

Interpretation: All currents are positive — our assumed directions were correct. The striking result is \(I_2 = 0\): no current flows through \(R_2\). The EMF difference \(\mathcal{E}_1 - \mathcal{E}_2 = 6.0\ \text{V}\) exactly matches the voltage that the \(R_1\)–\(R_3\) path sustains. If \(\mathcal{E}_2\) were even slightly different, current would flow through \(R_2\) — and could go in either direction.

Verification (outer loop): \(+\mathcal{E}_1 - I_1 R_1 - I_2 R_2 - \mathcal{E}_2 = 18.0 - 6.0 - 0 - 12.0 = 0\) ✓

27.4 — RC Circuits: Charging and Discharging

A New Kind of Circuit

Every circuit so far has been in steady state — currents constant in time. When a resistor and capacitor share a loop, something qualitatively new occurs: the current changes with time. The resistor limits how quickly charge flows onto (or off of) the capacitor, producing an exponential approach to equilibrium.

Charging an RC Circuit

Consider an uncharged capacitor \(C\) in series with resistor \(R\) and battery \(\mathcal{E}\). At \(t = 0\), we close the switch:

At \(t = 0\): The capacitor is uncharged (\(q = 0\)), so it acts like a short circuit — all the battery voltage appears across the resistor, and the initial current is at its maximum value:

\[I_0 = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\]

As \(t\) increases: Charge accumulates on the capacitor, building a voltage \(q/C\) that opposes the battery. This back-voltage increasingly fights the current, so the charging rate slows down. As \(t \to \infty\): The capacitor voltage reaches \(\mathcal{E}\), the opposition is complete, and current stops — the fully charged capacitor acts like an open circuit.

We can make this precise. Applying the loop rule at any time \(t\):

\[\mathcal{E} - IR - \frac{q}{C} = 0\]

Since \(I = dq/dt\), this becomes a first-order differential equation whose solution (verified by substitution) is:

\[\boxed{q(t) = Q_\text{max}\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)}, \qquad \boxed{I(t) = I_0\,e^{-t/RC}}\]

where \(Q_\text{max} = C\mathcal{E}\) is the final charge and \(I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R\) is the initial current. The solution confirms what the physics predicted: charge rises from zero toward \(Q_\text{max}\), current decays from \(I_0\) toward zero, both on the same exponential timescale.

Discharging an RC Circuit

Now suppose the capacitor is fully charged to \(Q_0\) and the battery is removed. The capacitor discharges through \(R\). The loop rule gives \(dq/dt = -q/(RC)\), with solution:

\[\boxed{q(t) = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}}, \qquad \boxed{I(t) = -\frac{Q_0}{RC}\,e^{-t/RC}}\]

The negative sign indicates current flows opposite to the charging direction — charge is leaving the capacitor.

TA note: Here \(Q_0\) is the charge on the capacitor at the instant discharge begins. If the capacitor was fully charged, \(Q_0 = Q_\text{max} = C\mathcal{E}\); if charging was interrupted before completion, \(Q_0 < Q_\text{max}\). The discharge equation is general — it does not assume the capacitor started fully charged.

The Time Constant

\[\boxed{\tau = RC}\]

*Personal note: The dimensional analysis is worth doing explicitly: \([\Omega][\text{F}] = (\text{V/A})(\text{C/V}) = \text{C/A} = \text{s}\). Resistance slows the flow; capacitance sets how much charge must flow. Their product is a time.

The time constant sets the characteristic timescale:

Time Charging: \(q/Q_\text{max}\) Discharging: \(q/Q_0\)
\(t = \tau\) 63.2% 36.8%
\(t = 2\tau\) 86.5% 13.5%
\(t = 3\tau\) 95.0% 5.0%
\(t = 5\tau\) 99.3% 0.7%

Charging vs. Discharging: A Comparison

Quantity Charging Discharging
\(q(t)\) \(Q_\text{max}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})\) \(Q_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\)
\(I(t)\) \(I_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\) \(-(Q_0/RC)\,e^{-t/\tau}\)
\(q\) at \(t = 0\) \(0\) \(Q_0\)
\(I\) at \(t = 0\) \(I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R\) \(-Q_0/RC\)
\(q\) at \(t \to \infty\) \(Q_\text{max} = C\mathcal{E}\) \(0\)

Energy in RC Charging: The 50% Result

During charging, the battery delivers total energy \(U_\text{battery} = Q_\text{max}\,\mathcal{E} = C\mathcal{E}^2\). The energy stored in the fully charged capacitor is \(U_C = \frac{1}{2}C\mathcal{E}^2\) — exactly half. The other half is dissipated as heat in the resistor. This 50% efficiency is a fundamental result, independent of \(R\), \(C\), and \(\mathcal{E}\).

*Personal note: No matter how small you make \(R\), you still lose half the energy to heat. The only way to improve efficiency is to use an inductor instead of a resistor to limit the current — a topic for Chapter 31.

Example: An RC Circuit

\(R = 8.00 \times 10^5\ \Omega\), \(C = 5.00\ \mu\text{F}\), \(\mathcal{E} = 12.0\ \text{V}\).

Time constant: \(\tau = RC = (8.00 \times 10^5)(5.00 \times 10^{-6}) = \boxed{4.00\ \text{s}}\)

Maximum charge: \(Q_\text{max} = C\mathcal{E} = \boxed{60.0\ \mu\text{C}}\)

Initial current: \(I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R = 12.0/(8.00 \times 10^5) = \boxed{15.0\ \mu\text{A}}\)

At \(t = \tau\): \(q = 60.0(1 - e^{-1}) = \boxed{37.9\ \mu\text{C}}\), \(I = 15.0\,e^{-1} = \boxed{5.52\ \mu\text{A}}\)

27.5 — Household Circuits and Electrical Safety

Household appliances are wired in parallel across the 120 V supply. Each device gets the full voltage; the currents add at the breaker panel:

\[I_\text{total} = \frac{P_1}{\Delta V} + \frac{P_2}{\Delta V} + \cdots\]

A circuit breaker (15 A or 20 A) opens the circuit if \(I_\text{total}\) exceeds the safe limit. For a 120 V / 15 A circuit: \(P_\text{max} = 1800\ \text{W}\). This is why you can’t run a 1500 W heater and a 1300 W microwave on the same circuit — their combined 23.3 A exceeds the breaker.

A short circuit creates a near-zero resistance path, producing enormous current (\(I = \mathcal{E}/r_\text{wire}\)) and heat. The breaker protects the wiring from fire. A ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) detects current imbalances as small as 5 mA — indicating leakage through an unintended path (possibly a person) — and trips in milliseconds. The breaker protects the wiring; the GFCI protects you.

*Personal note: Both devices apply Kirchhoff’s junction rule to fault conditions. The breaker monitors total current; the GFCI monitors the difference between hot and neutral. Same physics, different failure modes.

27.6 — Measuring Instruments

An ammeter measures current and must be placed in series. For accurate measurement, it must have very low resistance (\(R_A \approx 0\)) so inserting it does not significantly reduce the current.

A voltmeter measures potential difference and must be placed in parallel. It must have very high resistance (\(R_V \approx \infty\)) so it draws negligible current.

The measurement paradox: No real instrument is ideal. A real ammeter (\(R_A > 0\)) reduces the current; a real voltmeter (\(R_V < \infty\)) lowers the voltage. Both instruments perturb the circuit they measure — the ideal ammeter is a perfect wire, the ideal voltmeter a perfect open circuit, and every real instrument lives somewhere between.

27.7 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. EMF and terminal voltage: A real battery has \(\Delta V = \mathcal{E} - Ir\), always less than \(\mathcal{E}\) when current flows.

  2. Series resistors: \(R_\text{eq} = \sum R_i\). Same current; voltages add. Equivalent is larger than the largest.

  3. Parallel resistors: \(1/R_\text{eq} = \sum 1/R_i\). Same voltage; currents add. Equivalent is smaller than the smallest.

  4. Kirchhoff’s Junction Rule (KCL): \(\sum I_\text{in} = \sum I_\text{out}\) — charge conservation.

  5. Kirchhoff’s Loop Rule (KVL): \(\sum \Delta V = 0\) — energy conservation.

  6. RC circuits: Time constant \(\tau = RC\). Charging: \(q = Q_\text{max}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})\), \(I = I_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\). Discharging: \(q = Q_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\). During charging, exactly half the battery’s energy is dissipated in the resistor.

  7. Ammeters (series, low \(R\)) and voltmeters (parallel, high \(R\)) both perturb the circuit they measure.

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Terminal voltage \(\Delta V = \mathcal{E} - Ir\)
Series resistance \(R_\text{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \cdots\)
Parallel resistance \(1/R_\text{eq} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3 + \cdots\)
Junction rule (KCL) \(\sum I_\text{in} = \sum I_\text{out}\)
Loop rule (KVL) \(\sum \Delta V = 0\)
RC charging: charge \(q(t) = Q_\text{max}(1 - e^{-t/RC})\), where \(Q_\text{max} = C\mathcal{E}\)
RC charging: current \(I(t) = I_0\,e^{-t/RC}\), where \(I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R\)
RC discharging: charge \(q(t) = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}\)
RC discharging: current \(I(t) = -(Q_0/RC)\,e^{-t/RC}\)
Time constant \(\tau = RC\)

Looking Ahead

In Chapter 28, we enter entirely new territory: magnetic fields and magnetic forces. We will discover that moving charges not only respond to electric fields but also create and respond to magnetic fields. The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field, \(\vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\), has a remarkable property: it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion without changing the speed. This leads to circular orbits, the deflection of current-carrying wires, and ultimately to electric motors.

*With Kirchhoff’s rules, we can analyze any circuit in steady state. But the most interesting phenomena in electromagnetism arise when things change — when currents vary, when charges accelerate, when fields evolve in time. The magnetic field is our gateway to that richer, dynamic world.
